summary: A Toptenz.net list article by Elizabeth Fickenscher counting down 10 psychological phenomena, each with a definition and a real-world example. The entries cover cryptomnesia, deja vu, the bystander effect, the placebo effect, the McGurk effect, the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, cognitive dissonance, the online disinhibition effect, reverse psychology, and the overview effect. Website boilerplate, sidebars and related-article links are ignored.
one_line: A Toptenz.net countdown of ten psychological phenomena, from cryptomnesia and deja vu to cognitive dissonance and the overview effect, with real-world examples.
key_facts: Cryptomnesia was named by doctors Alan Brown and Dana Murphy after three experiments at Southern Methodist University in 1989.
A judge decided that cryptomnesia was the culprit in George Harrison's 'My Sweet Lord' and Harrison was charged with 'subconscious plagiarism'.
French psychiatrist Francois-Leon Arnaud wrote about a 19th-century soldier named Louis who suffered almost constant deja vu.
Kitty Genovese was murdered in 1964, and the article says the 38 bystanders who witnessed the murder did nothing to help, though only a few actually saw the attack.
Topsy the Elephant was electrocuted on Coney Island in front of many witnesses, and nobody lifted a finger to help.
Merck developed the experimental antidepressant MK-869 in 2002, and those who took the placebo felt just as better as those who took MK-869.
About 50% of developing drugs fail in the trial stage because the placebo is found to be just as effective, according to the article.
The McGurk Effect was first explained in 1976 by a researcher named McGurk who studied how infants perceive language.
Arnold Swicky, a linguistics professor at Stanford, named the Frequency Illusion in 2006, which is also known as the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon.
Leon Festinger first studied cognitive dissonance in 1957 using a doomsday cult that believed a flood would end the world.
The Online Disinhibition Effect describes people saying or typing things they would not usually say in real life, often when they feel anonymous.
Antoine-Augustin Parmentier ate potatoes while imprisoned during the Seven Years' War, and French Parliament outlawed potatoes in 1748 because they were thought to cause leprosy.
Frank White created the term Overview Effect to describe astronauts' experience of seeing the Earth as part of something bigger.
Six astronauts were interviewed by Inverse about the Overview Effect.
